title: Linked Lists: Singly and Doubly Connected Structures
description: This module introduces learners to Linked Lists—linear data structures where elements (nodes) are stored in non-contiguous memory and linked via pointers. We'll begin with the fundamentals of singly linked lists, including node creation, insertion, deletion, and traversal. Then, we explore the more versatile doubly linked lists, which allow bi-directional navigation. Through visual aids, code examples, and hands-on problems, students will build a strong intuition for dynamic memory structures and use cases like implementing stacks, queues, and even undo-redo functionality.

lessons.title: Introduction to Linked Lists
lessons.content:
A **Linked List** is a linear data structure where each element (called a node) contains two parts:
- `data`: The value
- `next`: A pointer/reference to the next node

Unlike arrays, linked lists do not use contiguous memory. This allows efficient insertion and deletion, especially in the middle or beginning of the list.

Types:
- **Singly Linked List**: Each node links to the next
- **Doubly Linked List**: Each node links to both next and previous nodes
- **Circular Linked List**: Last node links back to the first

Linked lists are used in:
- Dynamic memory allocation
- Implementing stacks/queues
- Navigating browser history
- Undo-redo in editors

Introduction to Doubly Linked Lists
lessons.content:
**Doubly Linked Lists** allow navigation both forwards and backwards by adding a `prev` pointer to each node. This is useful in scenarios like:
- Browser back/forward navigation
- Music players (next/previous song)
- Undo-redo operations

Each node contains:
- `data`: the value
- `next`: pointer to the next node
- `prev`: pointer to the previous node

Doubly linked lists consume more memory but are more versatile in editing operations.

Linked List vs Array: When and Why
lessons.content:
**Linked Lists** vs **Arrays**:

| Feature            | Array                  | Linked List             |
|--------------------|------------------------|--------------------------|
| Memory Allocation | Contiguous             | Non-contiguous          |
| Access Time       | O(1) via index         | O(n) via traversal       |
| Insertion         | O(n) (worst case)      | O(1) at head             |
| Deletion          | O(n) (worst case)      | O(1) with pointer access |
| Memory Overhead   | Low                    | High (extra pointers)    |

Use **linked lists** when:
- Frequent insertions/deletions in the middle
- Unknown size upfront
- You need dynamic memory

Use **arrays** when:
- Fast random access is required
- Memory efficiency is important
